NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION) — The question-answered sentence is: "A dual-lumen catheter design with integrated microfluidic pressure-sensing channels that actively monitors infusion pressure at multiple points along the catheter length." Standard practice uses a single-lumen catheter with pressure sensing only at the pump outlet, which cannot detect kinks or partial occlusions downstream. This intervention differs from adjacent techniques (like catheter reinforcement or material changes) by introducing distributed sensing through microfluidic channels that create a pressure wave pattern signature, allowing detection of specific failure mechanisms without raising nuisance alarms. The mechanism attacks the failure's driving physics by creating a baseline pressure signature that changes predictably when kinking, fibrin deposition, or air emboli occur at any point along the catheter, enabling early detection of partial obstructions before they become complete occlusions.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing physical relation is based on the Hagen-Poiseuille equation for pressure drop in tubes: ΔP = (8μLQ)/(πr⁴), where ΔP is pressure drop, μ is viscosity, L is length, Q is flow rate, and r is radius. By introducing microfluidic channels that branch from the main infusion lumen at 10cm intervals, we create a distributed pressure sensing network. A partial occlusion at position x will cause a characteristic pressure wave pattern that differs from a complete occlusion or kink. For a 20% partial occlusion, the pressure drop increases by approximately 56% (since ΔP ∝ 1/r⁴), which is detectable as a localized pressure anomaly in the microfluidic network. This distributed sensing reduces the detection threshold for partial occlusions from the current system's fixed pressure threshold to a dynamic baseline that can detect small changes.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — 
Standard practice components:
- Single-lumen catheter (90cm, medical-grade silicone)
- Standard infusion set connector
- Insulin reservoir connection
- Adhesive mounting system

Proposed intervention components:
- Dual-lumen catheter (90cm, medical-grade silicone) - replaces standard catheter
- Microfluidic pressure sensing channels (integrated into catheter wall) - added feature
- Pressure wave pattern analysis algorithm (software update to pump controller) - replaces existing occlusion detection algorithm
- Miniature pressure transducers at pump end (3 units) - added to pump housing
- Calibration fluid reservoir (5ml) - added to pump system

All components are procurable through existing medical device suppliers. The microfluidic channels can be manufactured using existing catheter extrusion techniques with minor tooling modifications. The software update runs on the existing pump controller hardware.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) — 
| Component/Feature | Standard Practice | Proposed Intervention | Burden Impact |
|-------------------|-------------------|----------------------|--------------|
| Catheter | Single-lumen silicone | Dual-lumen with microfluidic channels | Same material, minor manufacturing change |
| Pump Controller | Fixed pressure threshold algorithm | Pattern recognition algorithm | Software update only, no hardware change |
| Sensors | Single pressure sensor at outlet | Three pressure transducers at inlet | Added sensors but within existing pump housing |
| Calibration | None | Small calibration reservoir | Minimal added volume |
| Manufacturing | Standard extrusion | Modified extrusion with additional channels | Minor tooling change |
| Cost | Standard catheter cost | 15-20% higher catheter cost | Within same cost class |
| Complexity | Simple occlusion detection | Pattern recognition | Software complexity increase but no hardware penalty |

Conclusion: Same burden class - all changes are within existing manufacturing and cost infrastructure, with only software and minor catheter modifications required.

EXECUTABLE TEST — 
Protocol: Test 50 catheters under simulated ambulatory conditions with controlled introduction of kinks, fibrin deposits, and air emboli at various positions along the catheter length.

Instruments:
- Test pump with prototype controller
- Pressure monitoring system with 10 sensors along catheter length
- Glucose monitoring simulator
- Mechanical kinking device
- Fibrin deposition simulator
- Air injection system

Procedure:
1. Baseline calibration: Establish normal pressure wave signature for each catheter
2. Introduce kinks at 30cm, 60cm, and 90cm positions (5 catheters each)
3. Introduce partial occlusions (20%, 40%, 60%) at 20cm, 50cm, and 80cm positions (5 catheters each)
4. Introduce air emboli of 0.5ml, 1ml, and 2ml volumes (5 catheters each)
5. Record time to detection and false positive rate over 14-day wear period

Pass/Fail Criteria:
- Complete occlusion detection within 15 minutes (100% pass rate required)
- Partial occlusion (20%+) detection within 2 hours (95% pass rate required)
- Nuisance alarm rate ≤1 per 14 days (pass rate required)
- No missed insulin delivery events >20% deficit (100% pass rate required)

Duration: 14 days per catheter, with tests running simultaneously on all 50 catheters
Kill Criterion: If any test category fails to meet pass criteria, the intervention is rejected and must be redesigned.
